Adaptation: The decrease in the frequency of action potentials (firing rate) by a sensory receptor over time when subjected to a constant, unchanging stimulus (e.g., tonic receptors adapt slowly, phasic receptors adapt rapidly).
Describe the role of voltage gated action potentials (potassium and sodium) in the generation of an action potential.

qs.q: An experiment shows that blocking sodium channels prevents the generation of action potentials. What is the primary role of sodium influx during the depolarization phase?
o: Membrane repolarization phase
Rapid membrane depolarization
After-hyperpolarization generation
Resting potential maintenance
Neurotransmitter release inhibition
qs.e: The influx of sodium ions causes a rapid shift in membrane potential, leading to depolarization.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Neurophysiology I Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An experiment demonstrates that blocking potassium channels prolongs the action potential. What is the primary role of potassium efflux during repolarization?
o: After-depolarization generation
Membrane depolarization phase
Resting potential restoration
Threshold potential maintenance
Sodium channel inhibition
qs.e: Potassium efflux restores the negative membrane potential, completing the repolarization phase.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Neurophysiology I Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: During a patch-clamp experiment on a neuron, extracellular sodium is replaced entirely by an inert impermeant cation. What happens to the peak of the subsequent action potential?
o: It shifts toward a hyperpolarized value matching the potassium equilibrium.
It undergoes rapid damped oscillations before stabilizing at zero mV.
It remains completely unchanged because potassium drives the rising phase.
It becomes significantly larger due to altered internal driving forces.
It fails to overshoot and peaks closer to the resting membrane level.
qs.e: Removing extracellular sodium eliminates the inward sodium current, preventing the membrane potential from reversing and overshooting zero.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Neurophysiology I Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A motor neuron is subjected to a prolonged threshold depolarizing stimulus. Why does the frequency of action potential firing eventually adapt or slow down over time?
o: Sodium channel inactivation gates close permanently throughout the sustained depolarization.
Membrane capacitance gradually rises because of expansion of the lipid bilayer.
Intracellular ATP becomes depleted, stopping the activity of ion‑transport pumps.
Extracellular calcium levels increase, thereby blocking the inward depolarizing current.
Voltage‑gated potassium channels activate slowly, producing a hyperpolarizing afterpotential.
qs.e: Spike frequency adaptation is primarily caused by the slow accumulation of open voltage-gated potassium channels maintaining a hyperpolarizing afterpotential.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Neurophysiology I Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: In a study of myelinated nerve fibers, a localized focal demyelination event occurs at a single internode. What is the immediate functional consequence for action potential propagation?
o: Conduction stops completely because the internode lacks any active ion channels.
Propagation speed decreases locally as current leaks across the exposed membrane.
Conduction velocity rises because membrane capacitance at the node is reduced.
The impulse reverses direction and travels backward toward the neuronal soma.
Action potential amplitude doubles to compensate for the reduced resistance.
qs.e: Demyelination reduces membrane resistance and increases capacitance at the affected site, causing current leak that slows or halts saltatory conduction.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Neurophysiology I Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An experimental animal is infused with an enteric peptide that triggers strong action potentials over the plateau of slow waves in the gastric antrum. Which primary ion influx is directly responsible for generating these spike potentials?
o: Voltage-dependent calcium channel flux
Ligand-gated potassium current entry
Slow calcium sodium channel movement
Fast sodium channel activation
Cyclic nucleotide channel stimulation
qs.e: Gastrointestinal spike potentials are true action potentials caused mainly by calcium-sodium influx through slow channels.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Physiology Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: During an action potential in a large myelinated axon, a neurophysiologist blocks the repolarizing current. Which specific ionic movement is directly prevented by this experimental intervention?
o: Inward sodium flow through inactivation gate closures
Outward potassium flow through voltage-gated channels
Uptake of calcium via internal store release sites
Entry of chloride through ligand-activated membrane gates
Removal of magnesium block at resting membrane potentials
qs.e: Repolarization of the nerve cell membrane is primarily driven by the outward flow of potassium ions.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Physiology Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A study shows that blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in a neuron prevents action potential initiation. What is the primary mechanism of this block?
o: Inhibition of depolarization phase
Enhancement of repolarization phase
Increase of potassium permeability
Decrease of chloride conductance
Stabilization of resting potential
qs.e: Sodium channels are crucial for the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Neurophysiology I Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: An action potential is a rapid, all‑or‑nothing change in membrane potential that propagates along excitable cells, enabling nerve impulses and muscle contraction. It is driven by voltage‑gated ion channels and is essential for coordinated cardiac and nervous function.

sections.p: An action potential is a brief, large depolarization of a cell membrane that travels along the cell, allowing rapid communication between cells.
b: All‑or‑nothing: either a full spike or none

sections.p: Depolarization opens voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels, causing Na⁺ influx. Repolarization follows with K⁺ efflux through voltage‑gated K⁺ channels. In cardiac cells, Ca²⁺ influx sustains the plateau.

t.b: Shows characteristic phases of cardiac AP; abnormal patterns suggest channelopathies.

sections.p: The refractory period, modulated by ion channel kinetics, prevents back‑propagation and ensures unidirectional conduction. Autonomic tone adjusts channel activity.

t.b: Detects conduction delays or blocks; abnormal intervals indicate channel dysfunction.

sections.p: Mutations in ion channel genes, electrolyte imbalances, or drug effects can alter AP shape, leading to arrhythmias or muscle weakness.

t.b: Prolonged QT predicts torsades de pointes risk.
Low K⁺ shortens AP, causing arrhythmias; high K⁺ prolongs AP.

sections.p: AP abnormalities manifest as arrhythmias, syncope, or sudden death. Recognizing patterns guides drug choice and urgent interventions.

t.b: Identifies paroxysmal arrhythmias; informs antiarrhythmic selection.
Elevated LDH may indicate myocardial injury affecting AP.

sections.p: Remember the all‑or‑nothing principle and the distinct phases of cardiac AP. Know how drugs like amiodarone prolong AP by blocking K⁺ channels.

t.b: Blocks K⁺ channels, prolongs repolarization, increases refractory period.

faq.q: What causes a prolonged QT interval?
faq.a: Electrolyte disturbances, certain drugs, congenital channelopathies, or structural heart disease.

faq.q: Why does hypokalemia lead to arrhythmias?
faq.a: Low K⁺ shortens repolarization, increasing excitability and risk of early afterdepolarizations.

faq.q: How does amiodarone affect the action potential?
faq.a: It blocks K⁺ channels, prolonging phase 3, thereby increasing refractory period and reducing arrhythmia recurrence.

exam: Explain the phases of a cardiac action potential and how they differ from a neuronal AP.
Describe how hypokalemia alters the action potential and the clinical consequences.
Discuss the mechanism of action of amiodarone and its impact on the cardiac action potential.
